body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students explain how cultural patterns and economic decisions shaped and were shaped by environments of forest, lake and mountain (D2.Geo.4.6-8), and how farming methods let settlement grow (D2.Geo.8.6-8).
- Students analyze how Bernal Diaz's perspective and purpose shaped his account (D2.His.6.6-8, RH.6-8.6), detect limits in a record written by the conquerors (D2.His.10.6-8), and relate the primary source to a secondary reading on the same topic (RH.6-8.9).
- Students organize evidence into a coherent argument and support claims with relevant, accurate evidence (D2.His.16.6-8, WHST.6-8.1.B).

MATERIALS
- Three Civilizations, Three Environments (lesson reading)
- A Spanish Soldier Remembers Tenochtitlan (primary source, adapted)
- A map of Mesoamerica and the Andes, and a physical map of the Valley of Mexico showing Lake Texcoco
- Images of a chinampa, Inca terraces, a quipu, and Maya glyphs (from a museum's free educational collection)
- A three-column comparison chart: environment, adaptation, achievement

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read the overview. Show images of the three environments. Begin the lesson, Three Civilizations, Three Environments, with students filling in the comparison chart as they read.
Day 2: Finish the lesson. Short discussion of evidence: what do we learn from archaeology, Maya inscriptions, quipus, Aztec codices and Spanish accounts?
Day 3: Read the Diaz excerpts aloud. Students complete A Soldier Remembers Tenochtitlan, focusing on when and why Diaz wrote.
Day 4: Seminar: what is missing from Diaz's account, and where might historians find Mexica voices (codices, accounts recorded in Nahuatl after the conquest, archaeology)? Students plan their arguments.
Day 5: Assessment: The Greatest Achievement. Close the semester with a quick write connecting one achievement to Mesopotamia, the Silk Roads, Baghdad, Mali or medieval Europe.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a partially completed comparison chart and image cards for chinampa, terrace and quipu. Offer the frame "Diaz was amazed by ___. He may have written this because ___."
- Support: let students write the assessment as a structured paragraph set (claim, two evidence paragraphs, counterclaim) with headings.
- Stretch: compare Diaz's description of the market with what archaeologists have found at Tlatelolco, or research how scholars are still deciphering Maya writing.
- Multilingual learners: pre-teach causeway, tribute and conquest with images; point out Nahuatl words used in English (chocolate, tomato, avocado); allow a home-language discussion before writing the claim.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
Our last unit is the Americas before 1500: the Maya, with their writing and calendars; the Aztecs, with their island city of Tenochtitlan and its floating gardens; and the Inca, with their mountain roads and knotted-cord records called quipus. Your child will also read a Spanish soldier's memory of Tenochtitlan and think about whose stories get written down. Ask your child which achievement they find most impressive, and why. Several foods we eat every day, such as chocolate, tomatoes and potatoes, were first grown in the Americas.
title: Teacher guide: The Americas Before 1500
